item.title: The Go Bag Edition
item.description: On thoughtful preparedness, planning, and removing the prepper stigma
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
This is one of the highest performing posts we’ve ever done. And it seems particularly relevant these days. Resurfacing for your weekend. -Colin (CJN)

Chris P. (CP) and Brady M. (BJM) are WITI contributors and former Special Forces soldiers: Brady was an Officer (18A MOS) and Chris was a Weapons Sergeant (18B MOS). The notoriously tough Green Beret training pipeline and real-life deployments put them in some unfriendly places, and we asked them to write about what average people should be thinking about when it comes to disaster preparation. It’s important to move from the “crazy prepper” stigma into widespread awareness of what to do when things go bad, quickly. Here’s a list of very pragmatic things to do and think about, from two guys that know.

Brady and Chris here. In Season 3 of The Simpsons, Moe Szyslak, the neighborhood bartender, steals a secret cocktail recipe from Homer that includes cough syrup. It makes his bar amazingly popular, but he’s required to both keep the recipe secret and bring in enough cough syrup to serve his growing customer base. When some regulars spy him wheeling cases of medicine into the back of the bar, he deflects attention telling them “Heh...I got hooked on the stuff in the service!”

This is how I explain some of the admittedly odd things I still do after leaving the Army over a decade and change ago—I got hooked on them in the service. One of the biggest habits I still have is a tendency towards over-preparing for emergencies. This manifests itself as carrying around a survival kit and a small med bag most of the time. Like your grandparents who keep calls short because of long-distance phone fees, I got this habit from painful survival school lessons and working overseas in rough neighborhoods.

The truth today is that, as a people, we have become remarkably dependent on technology. Try getting around without your smartphone and debit or credit cards for 12 hours and see what I mean. What this has created is a massive vulnerability—it means that if something like our power grid were interrupted and large urban areas went dark for days, it could become really difficult for everyone around you to get by. The worry is that if this happens a dense urban population could begin to panic, making things much worse. The best option often could be simply leaving as soon as possible for a spot not so tightly packed until things get better. Doing this would require an individual to be prepared in advance for that departure. “Never have anything in your life that you can’t walk out on in thirty seconds flat if you spot the heat coming around the corner” is a good piece of advice if you want to avoid a bad situation.

Why is this interesting?

Thirty seconds flat means you need to pack what’s needed and keep it where you can easily reach it and hit the road. Having the right stuff in the bag is key—a “go-bag” makes it easy because you’ve planned ahead of time and don’t have to think. Here’s what we recommend:

  1. A simple backpack. Keep it low key, camo or military webbing on the outside signals that you’ve got a backpack full of survival kit, and we don’t want that. Nobody at work is going to wonder about the dingy Jansport you keep stuffed under your desk.

  2. At least one durable, full water bottle. This can also make an airtight container for some of your water-sensitive kit as well as good for drinking water. Chris uses Nalgene. Brady uses Kleen Kanteen. Purification tablets or a purification straw are a must as well.

  3. Gorilla Tape. Don’t buy any other brand. To save on space and weight, we just wrap a few feet around the water bottle. Good for a hundred uses, repairs, bandages, cordage, etc.

  4. A Multitool. There are plenty of bladeless options out there that are safe for work. The pliers, scissors, and screwdrivers have a million uses. I got issued the Gerber MP600 back in 2003 and it’s all I’ve used ever since—it’s a great balance of simplicity, durability and the ability to open one-handed. (BJM)

  5. A Knife. “A Knifeless Man Is a Lifeless Man,” as the Faroese Proverb goes. This is much less as a weapon, and much more as the ultimate utility. A knife is a tool that can make other tools. Choose one that holds an edge and is still easy to sharpen. I’ll make your search for the best blade simpler by recommending a Mora knife—they’re incomparably inexpensive, come scary sharp and the Scandinavian grind means they’re much simpler to sharpen than others. Level II preparedness: Get a sharpening stone and learn how to sharpen. Could save your life one day.

  6. Flashlight. We strongly encourage you to have a headlamp with a red light option. The red light is good for lighting your way without shouting to the world your location—and it doesn’t ruin your limited natural ability to see in the dark as bad as white light does. Don’t keep batteries inside this lamp as they can corrode.

  7. A couple sets of spare batteries is key. Lithiums are great, alkalines are fine.

  8. Map with a couple routes home drawn on them. This can get complicated and a lot of people now use GPS, but relying only on your smartphone alone to navigate is a bad idea—even in low-level emergencies, the communications network can be co-opted by emergency services. We prefer 1:24,000 or 1:50,000 Scale USGS maps (good scales for moving on foot), available on paper for under $20 apiece. A small but reliable compass is also good for getting your bearings in unfamiliar territory.

  9. Phone necessities. Spare battery, charging cable, and even solar charging panels. Don’t neglect your smartphone—if it works, it could be a lifesaver. Even if phone lines are jammed, text messages can queue and oftentimes a GPS will work even without a fully functional cell network. Level II preparedness: in “emergency” or battery conserving mode I power my phone off except for 5min on the hour, every hour. This “comms window” can be used to check in with family or set a plan for other comms windows. (CPP)

  10. Spare shoes & socks. Nothing will end your trip home sooner than work shoe blisters and wet feet. This is actually the most important item in my packing list: a comfortable pair of walking shoes and two pairs of wool hiking socks. (CPP) You can’t do any better than Smartwool for comfort, durability, and water-resilience. (BJM)

  11. Cash money. A wad of $20s can get you food, water, transportation, and favors.

  12. A First Aid Kit. You can go with what we’ve recommended, or buy a pre-made one online. Either way, don’t forget a SOF-T or RATS Tourniquet and consider carrying two. Level II preparedness: Learn how to stop the bleeding in bad situations. This is where you’ll use SMARCH. (BJM)

  13. Fire-starting items. Staying warm when you can’t access modern heating will save your life, and it’s a hell of a lot more comfortable than freezing. I try to have at least 2 modes of fire-starting with me whenever possible—so that includes having a simple cheap Bic lighter as well as a fire steel. (BJM)

  14. Food. This isn’t just about staying alive - it’s about keeping a clear head in order to make good decisions. Choose food you can eat quickly on the move, and that of course won’t go bad right away. High calorie energy bars and Ensure aren’t a bad idea. Consider how many calories you normally consume in a day and have yourself covered for a couple days.

  15. A hat. Seems irrelevant, but it’s not. In cold weather, it’ll keep you from losing body heat, and in the summer it’ll prevent problems from overexposure. A baseball cap is fine.

  16. A layer. A lightweight layer can do wonders if it’s moisture-wicking and worn against the skin - meaning no cotton. A Polartec ECWCS Level I silkweight shirt is all I’ve used for nearly 20 years. Solid gold. (BJM)

  17. A raincoat. Being wet is bad, and being cold is bad. But being wet and cold is almost unbearable. It doesn’t need to be Goretex - it just needs to keep out the rain and wind.

Once you’ve got all this together, consider actually trying out at least your top 2 routes out of town as a rehearsal. As you’re rehearsing, try to visualize the likely conditions in an emergency - and that getting out on foot might be necessary. Make changes to your go-bag and plan based on what you come up with. It’s important to keep in mind that your exit, and preparing for it, are all focused on survival. Make sure what you’re doing at every stage helps achieve that goal. (CP/BJM)

Medical Kit of the Day:

We wrote about the contents of a good individual first aid kit this past summer. (BJM)

item.title: The Tokyo Cocktail Bars Edition
item.description: An expert’s guide, with my personal annotations (and a map.)
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
Colin here. One of my favorite bars in Tokyo is Virtu, at the Four Seasons Otemachi. Sure, there are deeper cuts, but I find the staff, the environment, and the hospitality to be some of the best in the world.

Why is this interesting?

On a recent visit, one of the excellent team members, Graham, provided a nicely designed list they give to guests who want to explore the city’s cocktail scene further. It has some great, very informed selections ranging from Ginza cocktail institutions to tiny neighborhood bars, hotel rooftops and live music venues; I’ve added a little personal context to each recommendation below.

We’ve also built an interactive map of them here: witiguides.com

Bar Libre + Bar Libre Ginza — Ikebukuro / Ginza
The Ikebukuro original combines classic Japanese bartending with Japanese fruit, distinctive vessels and inventive techniques. Its Ginza sibling brings the drinks into a basement filled with tropical plants.

Little Smith — Ginza
A Ginza institution since 1993, with a large horseshoe-shaped counter and unusually high ceilings. Tell the bartender what you like and let the drinks follow from there.

Quarter Room — Setagaya-Daita
Soran Nomura’s bar turns art history into cocktail inspiration, with drinks that have drawn on Warhol’s Flowers and Mondrian’s geometric paintings. His background in fragrance adds another dimension to the experience.

The Bvlgari Bar — Yaesu
On the Bvlgari Hotel’s 45th floor, a bar modeled on an Italian garden pavilion sits between two rooftop terraces. Mediterranean planting, cocktails and Tokyo spread out below.

Apollo Bar Ginza — Ginza
A bar that takes the details seriously, making its own soda, tonic water and ginger ale. The soundtrack is Tom Waits, chosen by the owner.

Mori Bar Gran — Ginza
Classic cocktails with a rooftop terrace and views toward Tokyo Tower and Skytree. The signature Mori Martini is the place to start.

Rock Fish — Ginza
The bartender’s sheet singles this one out for “Best Highball.” The specialty is whisky and soda served without ice in a thoroughly chilled glass, with close attention to every component.

Bar Orchard Ginza — Ginza
Choose a piece of seasonal fruit from the display and the bartender builds a cocktail around it. The results range from variations on classics to more experimental creations.

Punch Room Tokyo — Ginza
At the Tokyo EDITION, Ginza, punch gets a Japanese interpretation through local spirits, sake, green tea and regional spices. Order by the glass or share a silver punch bowl.

Rondo — Kagurazaka
A six-seat bar devoted to traditional Japanese bartending. Its name borrows from the musical form in which a theme returns with variations—a fitting idea for a place built around repeat visits.

Golden Gai — Shinjuku
A dense network of alleys filled with tiny, highly individual bars, many seating only five or six people. Each has its own character and clientele; some welcome newcomers, while others are members-only.

Bar High Five — Ginza
Hidetsugu Ueno’s bar is a reference point for Japanese cocktail craft. Drinks begin with a conversation about your preferences, with the team refining its recommendations as the evening unfolds.

Fuglen Tokyo — Tomigaya
The Tokyo outpost of the Oslo café and bar, furnished with vintage Norwegian pieces. Nordic coffee by day gives way to cocktails at night, including drinks made with Norwegian spirits.

Bauhaus — Roppongi
A rock institution where the bar staff also form the house band. The repertoire moves through classic rock, hard rock and metal, from Led Zeppelin and Queen to Nirvana and Oasis.

Bar Renri — Nihonbashi
Cocktails draw on regional Japanese ingredients and the neighborhood’s historic producers. The signature Renri brings together gin, genmaicha and mirin, making the local connections quite literal.

Bar Kasumicho Arashi — Nishiazabu
Set in the converted basement of a private house, with the atmosphere of a comfortable living room. Seasonal fresh-fruit cocktails are tailored to your preferred flavors and strength.

Tani — Shibuya
A small upstairs bar in Udagawacho with rare whiskies, carefully made cocktails and an informal atmosphere. Fourteen seats, including seven at the counter.

Blue Note Tokyo — Minami-Aoyama
The Tokyo outpost of New York’s Blue Note has hosted leading jazz musicians and artists from other genres since 1988. Plan the evening around a performance, with dinner and drinks alongside it.

Mizunara: In Tokyo — Kagurazaka
The Kagurazaka sibling of Hong Kong’s Mizunara: The Library, with Japanese and Scotch whisky alongside cocktails using shochu and awamori. It also makes a point of catering to a quiet afternoon drink.

Mixology Heritage — Hibiya
A bar in Hibiya Okuroji devoted to classic cocktails and vintage spirits, with veteran bartender Manabu Ito’s knowledge at its center. Bottles from different eras offer a way to explore familiar drinks.

Royal Bar — Marunouchi
The Palace Hotel’s intimate bar preserves the restored counter from its original 1961 incarnation. Dark wood, leather and velvet, with a history tied to the hotel’s first chief bartender, known as “Mr. Martini.”

The Bar at The Ritz-Carlton, Tokyo — Roppongi
Cocktails on the 45th floor, with expansive city views through floor-to-ceiling windows. The drinks bring Japanese ingredients into the framework of Western classics.

Happy drinking, from team WITI.

(CJN)

item.title: The Rebuilding MTV Edition
item.description: A rare interview with the brilliant, enigmatic creator known as ‘Flex.’
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
Colin here. When MTV shut down its 24/7 music video channels at the end of last year, an independent solo creator known as ‘Flex’ rebuilt the experience in just 48 hours with WantMyMTV.org.

The website is a free (and ad-free) archive of 113,000+ hand-curated music videos—up from ~20,000 at its January launch—as well as channels for different decades, plus Yo! MTV Raps, Headbangers Ball, and the original August 1, 1981 launch lineup in perfect order.

Why is this interesting?

For many reasons, but to me, it’s really the anti-algorithmic, hand-curated, one-person-vs-a-dead-institution of it all. So I spoke to Flex to learn a little more. Here’s our conversation, edited down.

Colin: You used to run a company, your day job is AI pipelines, and you do all of this from an apartment in Vlorë, Albania. How did you get there, and why Flex instead of your name?

Flex: A lot of what’s been written about me is speculation, so here’s the real version. I studied art history, then spent most of my working life as a gem and mineral dealer. I know that’s a strange pivot, but it’s the same instinct: finding beautiful things, figuring out what they are and where they came from, and putting them in front of people.

When COVID hit, like a lot of people I had to reinvent myself. I went deep into tech, digital art, smart contracts and AI pipelines. MTV Rewind is where all of it met: an art historian’s eye, a dealer’s sense of what’s worth keeping, and the tools to do it at scale. The Vlorë part is true. I build all of this from an apartment in Albania.

Flex is what people know me as in the web3 world, where I spent those COVID years building, and it stuck. The project was never supposed to be about me though and I had no idea it would be so popular... It’s about the videos and the people who made them.

Which video, seen at what age and in what room, is the reason this exists?

I can’t point to one video. As a skate punk, anything by Spike Jonze hit hard, and it’s hard not to be floored by The Pharcyde’s “Drop” or the Beastie Boys’ “Sabotage.” But the real reason is a feeling more than a video.

I grew up in a logging town in the woods of rural Oregon. From about 11 or 12, I’d come home every day, put MTV on in the background, and do homework and art while it played. It took me somewhere outside that small life in the woods, to other cities, other scenes, other ways of being a person. It ran straight from the videos into the late-night animation block and just kept going. It was the soundtrack to my whole day.

So the room is a living room in the Oregon woods, and “the video” is well.......all of them, one after another. That’s what I’m trying to rebuild: not a library you search, but a channel you leave on that takes you somewhere.

You’ve gone from 20,000 videos to 113,000 in ten months, roughly 300 a day. What does hand-curated mean at that pace, where does software do the sorting, and what have you refused to put on the air?

Software does the boring part. Every video is checked before it goes on the air: it has to play in an embed, it can’t be age-restricted, and it can’t be a fan edit, a lyric video or a reaction clip. A sweep runs over the whole library to catch videos that have died. One pass in July removed more than 4,000. What I pick by hand is what the software can’t judge: which channels exist, what goes on them, and in what order. The clearest thing I’ve refused is the static upload, a song playing over a single album cover. My rule is simple: no motion, not a music video.

Early MTV barely played Black artists, and Bowie pressed Mark Goodman on it on camera in 1983. Goodman is now your featured curator. How much of the old gatekeeping belongs in a preservation project, and have you two talked about it?

Not about that, no. Mark and I have talked a few times, mostly about the legacy of music television and what it was like to be there at the beginning. That started after the New York Times reached out to him for their piece on the project.

The early exclusion of Black artists is real, and it belongs in the history. It took Michael Jackson, and the fight over “Billie Jean,” before anything really moved. That’s part of how MTV changed, and part of how the culture changed with it. Music and the industry around it have always been messy and in motion, and they still are. A preservation project should keep the record of what MTV was, sins included.

Keeping the record is different from keeping the gatekeeping, though. We don’t gatekeep. I’ve worked to make MTV Rewind as broad as I can: channels built around different communities and different parts of the world, music television rebuilt from Brazil to Canada to Australia, so there’s something for everyone. The 1981 launch lineup plays exactly as it aired, because that’s history. The other hundred-plus channels are what it could have been.

Def Jam averages 2.77 seconds a shot and Warp 125, which would be about two shots in a four-minute video from the label behind “Come to Daddy.” Is that a real fingerprint, or is it picking up static album-art uploads? What else has the data shown you that a fan’s eye missed?

Good catch. It was album art and that part of the page needs to be updated. Warp’s 125 second average came from static uploads, where someone posts a track over a single album cover and the analysis reads it as one four-minute shot. I found it in October, wrote a rule (no motion, not a music video) and pulled 265 static cards out of the corpus, most of them Warp’s. Warp’s real average is 38.4 seconds a shot. That’s still the slowest of the labels we studied, and that part is a real fingerprint. Warp’s visuals are built to sit next to the music instead of competing with it, and that holds across their eras.

What the data shows that a fan’s eye misses: grunge’s lo-fi look isn’t a myth, it’s measurable. Sub Pop has the lowest motion of any major independent label in the corpus, and it holds across 800-plus videos. And Def Jam cuts every 2.77 seconds on average, the fastest of any label we studied. You can feel that watching, but now you can prove it.

Your research cards are graded against a rubric pegged to Chris Cunningham. What earns top tier, and which beloved video fails?

There’s no specific Cunningham rubric. Every video is judged on the same terms, and Cunningham is one director among many in the corpus. Tier I needs two things at once: the video has to matter historically, and it has to do something with the form. Take On Me, Sabotage, Vogue and Hurt all clear both bars easily. Being famous isn’t enough.

The best example of a beloved video that misses is Eddie Murphy’s “Party All the Time.” It went to #2, sat in heavy rotation on MTV and won an award. It’s a real cultural artifact. But visually it’s a performance in a recording studio, and the card puts it at Tier 1.5: chart and award significance, tempered by minimal visual experimentation. Journey’s “Any Way You Want It” lands in the same place for the same reason. It’s historically important, but it’s a band playing in a studio. Tier I is for the videos where the picture is doing as much work as the song.

Your FAQ treats the free site as the demo and RAD as the business, with label deals and licensing on top. Who’s buying, and what happens to “free forever” once a label is a client?

I’d push back a little on how that’s framed. The mission is preservation: keeping music videos and the culture around them watchable, findable and understood. RAD is a possible business layer that could fund that mission, but it isn’t the mission. If RAD never made a dollar, MTV Rewind would still be here and still be free.

Labels have started to show up. Tommy Boy, through Reservoir, is the first one. They pay for a clearly marked shelf that spotlights their catalog, plus aggregate reporting on how it performs. They send the playlist for their shelf, and honestly they’re great at it, because they know their own catalog from years of vinyl and reissue runs. That’s where their part ends. Our contract is explicit: they don’t buy any say in the curation, and they don’t own any rights to the software or to what plays on the site. The site stays free for viewers, with no ads, no algorithm and no login. If keeping it that way ever meant turning a client down, I’d turn them down.

You’re adding natural-language search to the corpus. Where’s your line between a tool that helps you see and the prediction engines you campaign against? Would you license this as training data?

I always say AI in the service of people, not people in the service of AI. Natural-language search is a way into the archive. It helps you find the slow-cut, high-contrast video you half remember. It doesn’t decide what you should watch next. We should never hand our own taste and judgment over to a machine. I’m an experimentalist at heart, so I spend a lot of time trying to understand these tools, partly out of plain curiosity and partly because no one’s reluctance has ever stopped the tide of progress. The job is to stay deliberate about how they’re used.

There’s no plan to license RAD as training data. What I’d love is for it to be used to teach music video history. That could eventually include building custom datasets for researchers in a specific field. Right now nearly 49,000 records are free to browse on RAD, and there’s no plan to ever close that off. A few instructors have told me they’ve already put it into their courses, and that’s the vision: a public good. These artifacts keep getting broken up by fractured rights and corporate interests that don’t value anything longer than a feed scroll. Somebody has to keep the record.

The archive runs on YouTube, which helped make music television unnecessary. When a video vanishes, what happens, and can it be an archive if someone else holds the files? Your FAQ also says you never store or copy the video files, so how did you measure 65,000 of them?

When a video disappears from YouTube, it drops off the channels. A sweep runs over the whole library to catch dead links, so viewers never hit a black screen. But the record of the video survives: who made it, who directed it, when, what it looked like, and why it mattered. RAD keeps that knowledge whether or not the file is still online.

So yes, I’d call it an archive, just not a vault. A library catalog doesn’t own the books to be useful, and a museum label tells you about a painting it didn’t paint. The files belong to the artists and labels who posted them. What we preserve is the context, the connections and the programming, and that’s the part most likely to be lost.

The visual data comes from software we wrote for the purpose. It analyzes each video and records measurements like cuts, shot length, motion, color and brightness. Those numbers are facts about the video, not the video. We never rehost, redistribute or sell anyone’s content. Everything you watch on MTV Rewind plays from where it’s publicly posted, and that’s a hard line in how the project is built.

Program 20 minutes for a WITI reader. Five videos, in order, and tell me why that order.

The Buggles, “Video Killed the Radio Star.” It’s the first video MTV ever played, and it’s a song about one medium killing off another. Pretty fitting for a project that exists because MTV walked away from its own music videos. You’ve got to start where it all started.

a-ha, “Take On Me.” This is when music videos stopped being promos and turned into art. The pencil sketch animation still holds up, and the art history nerd in me will never get tired of it.

The Pharcyde, “Drop.” Spike Jonze had them learn the whole song backwards, then shot it in reverse so it plays forward. Growing up a skate punk, Spike was a god to us, and honestly a video built on rewinding felt like the right thing to put in the middle of this.

Soundgarden, “Black Hole Sun.” Then it gets weird. Those melting grins, the suburban nightmare, the sun swallowing everybody whole. As a Pacific Northwest kid, this one hit close to home, and it was the late-night MTV that felt like you weren’t supposed to be seeing it. Chris Cornell was an alien, truly one of the last rock troubadours, and that’s a rare breed these days.

Beastie Boys, “Sabotage.” And you end on pure fun. Spike again, the fake ‘70s cop show, three of the best minutes MTV ever aired. You can’t watch it without grinning.

I put them in that order because that’s how MTV felt when you left it on all day. It starts with where it all began, gets artsy, gets strange late at night, and then sends you off on a high. It’s about 20 minutes, give or take.

Thanks for reading.

item.title: The Monday Media Diet with Hamish McKenzie
item.description: On Roll the Calls, ElevenReader, and Choke Enough
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
Hamish is a friend of WITI and one of the founders of Substack. He’s a former journalist, and author of the new book How to Save the Media, out November 17.

Tell us about yourself.

I grew up in a small, rural town in the south of New Zealand. In the winters, the high school boys tried to stay in shorts until it was far beyond reasonable. Many teenagers binge-drunk every weekend. The local culture was anchored on the phrase “harden up”. I was a decent student, particularly when it came to English and History, but it wasn’t until university that I was surrounded by people who thought intellectual achievement was a worthy goal. Still, even in high school I knew that I wanted to be a journalist. When I got to the University of Otago, I volunteered for the student magazine, Critic, right away. Later I became the editor. Then I went to do a master’s in journalism at the University of Western Ontario in Canada. I graduated and bolted to Hong Kong in pursuit of adventure and stories about China. I lived there for four years, and then followed my girlfriend back to her home country, the United States. She’s my wife now and we have two kids. We live in San Francisco and I have somehow ended up as the co-founder of a tech company that serves writers, journalists, and creators. I am 45 years old. I’m not quite sure how this all happened.

Describe your media diet.

I spend far too much time on both Substack Notes and X (guilty pleasure), with occasional forays into Reddit to make sure I’m really wasting my time well. For long form, I spend a lot of time with saved articles on Substack and diving into stories I find from the feed. The New York Times is my main news source, and I also read Stuff, the New Zealand Herald, and The Spinoff for news and commentary from the homeland. I listen to audiobooks, struggle through paper books, and flip through every issue of New York Magazine. I’m currently on podcast-listening rumspringa—I am getting slightly tired of the conversational-podcast format.

What’s the last great book you read?

When We Cease to Understand the World, by Benjamin Labatut. I actually read Labutut’s The MANIAC more recently, but it doesn’t touch the greatness of WWCTUTW, which was so innovative, alive, shocking, informative, and fantastically, tragically mad. Labutut rightly made those physicists more interesting and important than Picasso.

What are you reading now?

I’m listening to Ari Emanuel’s memoir Roll the Calls and inching my way through the delicious Anna Karenina, though it has been a few days since I’ve had a chance to pick it up.

What’s your reading strategy when you pick up a print copy of your favorite publication?

Lie on the couch, put my feet up on a cushion, fold the magazine’s pages and hold it up in one hand while I squint at text that is becoming increasingly elusive to my eyes. I breeze through the bite-sized stuff at the front and then pick a feature to dive into, inevitably being interrupted by my children before I reach the third page. Also, this scene almost never happens these days.

Who should everyone be reading that they’re not?

A couple of terrific but not especially well known Substack writers: Adam Mastroianni for fun and quirky science stories with a psychology bent; and Henrik Karlsson for thoughtful, artful, and calm-headed philosophies on how to live life well.

What is the best non-famous app you love on your phone?

I really like ElevenReader because it lets me listen to articles I haven’t had a chance to read with my eyes.

Plane or train?

Train. How can this even be a question? Trains are the greatest form of transportation ever known to man. The roominess. The vibrations. The landscapes rolling by at the perfect speed. Also, I’m terrified of dying in a plane crash.

What is one place everyone should visit?

I’m tempted to say a bunch of places in New Zealand, but a good part of their appeal is that they’re not overpopulated or overvisited, so instead I’ll say your grandmother’s place. That’s what everyone should do. Go visit their grandmother, if and when they can. You don’t get much time on the planet with your grandmother.

Tell us the story of a rabbit hole you fell deep into.

I’ve been absolutely loving Oklou’s Choke Enough, which I think is a Lux-tier album. But I realized after months of listening to it that I didn’t actually know anything about Oklou. So one night, I went on an Oklou bender, chasing her music videos and live performances across YouTube, reading her Wikipedia, listening to her back catalogue, and exploring the music of her collaborators, which led to another new favorite, Underscores. That was a very nice rabbit hole to fall into, and I’m still going down it.

item.title: The Saturday Selection, Vol. 129
item.description: Defining Indie, a retired Iger, trash can wheel rims, and much more.
item.dc:creator: Louis Cheslaw
item.content:encoded:

item.title: The Tokyu Hands Edition
item.description: On serendipity, retail, and bittersweet closings.
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
Colin here. Every Tokyo trip has a few fixed points for me, and one has always been the Hands store in Shibuya. (Wedged behind Parco, it’s still known as Tokyu Hands to anyone who’s been going for long enough.) I’d typically walk in to look at another Porter bag I didn’t need, and walk out two hours later with a better pencil sharpener, a card case (for my non-existent business cards), and other distinctly Japanese odds and ends. It was a cabinet of curiosities, and a fun rite of passage for Tokyo visitors.

But this Sunday, November 15, the store will close for good. Its lease is up, and after 48 years, the flagship will be no more. Hands (which the home improvement chain Cainz bought in 2022, dropping the “Tokyu”) will keep nearly 100 other stores, but Shibuya was the idea executed at the highest fidelity, with an estimated 100,000 SKUs unfurling up a hillside, across 24 split levels and 408 steps.

Why is this interesting?

The store started as a real estate problem. Tokyu Land had an awkward, L-shaped, sloping lot where a wooden church once stood, and decided to fill it with a new American import called DIY.

Yet the odd slope forced every floor into staggered A, B and C levels, meaning you corkscrew around the elevator, and soon completely lose track of where you are. In January, the company’s own chairman called it about the hardest building a retailer could work with.

But, like a casino, this disorientation was the part of the charm, and almost matched the overwhelm of the offering. (When it opened in 1978, Hands stocked 1,000 kinds of light bulbs and 3,000 carving chisels, graded from schoolchild to professional.)

Staff wore jeans and aprons, and many came from the trades, so they had a Home Depot-like level of actual understanding of what you might be trying to do. This astonishing depth held to the end, with around 100 nail clippers, 500 shoe care products and more than 1,000 bath salts on the floors this year.

In 2009 Hands named its approach with a slogan: “This is a Hint Market.” The underlying idea is that while a search box like Amazon rewards you for already knowing what you want, the magic of Hands was that it was built for browsing and puttering during the moment before you knew. The serendipity was the juice.

Back in January, celebrating 50 years and its best profits in three decades, Hands gathered journalists inside the Shibuya store to launch a campaign about getting lost on purpose. A pushback against Japan’s obsession with taipa, or time performance, the pitch was to wander and savor the time you were spending. But then, four months later, the closure notice came.

On October 29, a crane went up to the big green sign, and HANDS became THANKS, with the old Tokyu-era hand logo pulled out of retirement. Inside, staff built the main thank-you poster from strips of masking tape. The run of 48 thank-yous includes one to the skip floors, for getting everybody lost. (CJN)

item.title: The Solo Diner Edition
item.description: On rituals, hospitality, and decompression.
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re re-running this one from a few years back. It’s as true as ever. LC

Colin here. Keith McNally’s Instagram is full of charms and quirks, but what stands out to me is his longstanding loyalty to people who eat alone. Keith has mandated at all of his restaurants that patrons by themselves should be looked after, and never made to feel odd. The solo diner gets a glass of bubbles sent their way.

This stands in stark contrast: I recently called up Scott’s in London for a lunchtime table for one, and the thinly veiled repulsion from the other end of the line was bracing. It was short of the Dorsia laugh from American Psycho, but was sufficiently chilly in that perfect British way. (Fear not, gentle reader, I was soon welcomed into the Connaught with open arms).

Turns out, it’s no coincidence that I’ve typically received warm welcomes as a solo diner in NYC. It’s a delightfully New York thing. Noted restauranteur (and author of the superb book Unreasonable Hospitality) Will Giadara told Eater in 2018:

“I think it’s a real compliment,” New York City restaurateur Will Guidara says of solo guests. “It’s saying ‘I’m here at the restaurant. It’s my number one priority.’” Because of that enthusiasm, Guidara says that for those dining alone,“It is kind of a rule [at his NYC restaurant Eleven Madison Park] to go above and beyond to make those experiences special.”

Why is this interesting?

Treating a solo diner well is the essence of hospitality. It spurns the notion that a check could be bigger with a two-top, and focuses on the fact that solo dining can be a lovely, meditative experience, and also a sign of respect from the diner. Keith is not alone in his approach: Union Square Hospitality, run by friend of WITI Danny Meyer, also goes above-and-beyond for solo diners.

And it’s not a rare event for restaurants, either. A report from Seven Rooms showed that the number of people dining alone at NYC restaurants was on the rise a few years ago. Rightfully so! It is one of life’s great pleasures: with a book, lost in the scroll, or alone with your thoughts. With an ice cold, bone dry martini, West coast oysters, and a perfectly cooked filet in front of you, you can focus on the food and the ambience, and let everything come into crisp focus (or gently blur, depending on the martini consumption).

Writing about how a restaurant should view the solo diner, Eater critic Ryan Sutton hits the nail on the head. “If they believe in the power of the product, the power of their cuisine, should a restaurant not aim to be a complete, entertaining, and intellectually captivating experience all by itself?” (CJN)

item.title: The Monday Media Diet with Intern Pierre
item.description: On Kipling, Class: A Guide Through the American Status System, and Koufonisia
item.dc:creator: Intern Pierre
item.content:encoded:
Intern Pierre is the preferred luxury industry analyst of WITI. We like his obsession with ground truth, and also the general approach of speaking the truth about an industry that can read as a hall of mirrors. Read Alfred Tong’s piece for us here. Happy to have him with us this week. -Colin (CJN)

Tell us about yourself.

Don’t ask me to make plans for a month from now because I typically don’t know what I’m going to be doing or where I’ll be tomorrow.

My career started out in the MBB consulting world, where I mainly worked globally with institutional investors on due diligence work. Having had enough of my head wanting to explode from formal business jargon, circling back and people not knowing what they wanted, I moved into roles with hedge funds covering the consumer, tech and occasionally healthcare spaces. I really enjoyed working with the buy-side because it moved quickly and I was able to see the impact of my work.

I was fortunate enough to do well in that world, along with starting a business that I sold. My wife and I now split our time between Monaco and Spain, and I run a small family office.

Intern Pierre was started because I wanted to give regular industry professionals and retail investors access to information that professionals have access to (and pay quite a bit for). I really enjoy the luxury industry and felt that it wasn’t really covered well by the sell-side (UBS, Goldman, Morgan Stanley, etc.). Many industry journalists and commentators were either too emotional when it came to coverage, couldn’t really make a solid argument or had a conflict of interest, with many of the large luxury brands paying for advertising along with being directly or indirectly invested in the media publications.

As an example, CNBC boldly claimed that “Loud Luxury is Back” (it wasn’t then and it isn’t now), and Bloomberg was pushing articles on “Trader Joe’s Tote Bags” and “Slop Bowls” instead of covering underlying issues that were there if they had taken the time to have a look.

Intern Pierre has grown to be a great community of people. I’ve had the chance to meet several followers and subscribers, and it has resulted in some great new friendships all over the world. I am fortunate enough to be in a position where I can write what I think without having to worry about advertisers, investors or a management team, and I believe that gives me a different perspective that many people (with the exception of Bernard Arnault) seem to appreciate.

Aside from Intern Pierre, I enjoy travel, sailing, golf, wine, cooking and spending time with my friends and family.

Describe your media diet.

I am like a sponge when it comes to consuming information. I am able to read things quickly and remember details from them. During the day, this translates into a ton of information from Bloomberg alerts, X posts, Substack, WhatsApp messages, sell-side notes, data vendors, call transcripts, etc. Since I do most of my work in the luxury industry, publications like WWD and Business of Fashion (even though they’ve gone off a cliff) can be helpful here and there.

I will typically have the news on in the background throughout the day (I can’t stand working in a quiet space), and it changes consistently from European news to US news, Asian news and Middle East news. While I understand that pretty much all news sources are biased to an extent, it is helpful to read and listen to as much as you can to form an opinion.

I also spend a lot of time consuming information that is contradictory to my opinion or investment thesis. I believe that to form a solid opinion, you need to hear the other side. Who knows? Sometimes I even change my mind.

What’s the last great book you read?

Captains Courageous by Rudyard Kipling. My father read this to me when I was a child and, while it did take a while for me to understand, the message that you get from reading it is something I’ve carried with me.

If you’re not familiar, the story is about a very spoiled son of a wealthy railroad tycoon who is washed overboard on a transatlantic steamship. A fishing schooner, the We’re Here, rescues him and forces him to work off the debt he owes the crew for saving him (they didn’t believe he was wealthy) by serving as a cabin boy.

What are you reading now?

I try to read one or two books a week and just finished Class: A Guide Through the American Status System by Paul Fussell. An Intern Pierre follower recommended it based on a note that I wrote.

What’s your reading strategy when you pick up a print copy of your favorite publication?

I still enjoy reading many publications in print because it’s difficult to read on an iPad outside. I will typically take the Financial Times outside (with a glass of wine) and, after skimming through it, read what looks interesting uninterrupted.

Who should everyone be reading that they’re not?

While I do enjoy reading the Financial Times and find Bloomberg, WSJ, Reuters, etc., to be necessary for my day-to-day, I have found some of the best commentary on several things I cover to be on Substack. As I’ve written in the past, I believe we’re going to see a pivot to this platform, and if you’re credible and do good work, people will read and follow.

I have found “Arb Letter” by Arbitrage Andy (on Substack) to be very accurate when it comes to geopolitical events and understanding the view from the United States. While I don’t always agree with them, overall, the geopolitical coverage is differentiated and interesting to read.

I also have found “Rich People Shit” by Carson Griffith (also on Substack) to be entertaining and a fun read.

What is the best non-famous app you love on your phone?

SwingCore. My trainer built it and, while it’s still in beta, it’s a fantastic app to track progress and schedule training sessions. If I’m traveling, I can take a picture of the hotel gym, and it will give me workouts to do.

Most importantly, it gives you a Physical Handicap (like a golf handicap), which is based on workouts, data inputs, etc., so I can see how in shape I am compared to others in my demographic.

Plane or train?

This is tough; however, I would say nothing beats a train through the Alps in the winter (Paris to Milan, for example, is excellent). I love cars and don’t mind driving either.

Given the state of commercial air travel and my experience with it recently, long-haul flights are awful regardless of what section of the plane you’re in.

What is one place everyone should visit?

I really enjoy history, along with beautiful weather, so I would say, as a country, Greece. I hesitate to get specific on this because this place has started to get increasingly popular. However, Koufonisia, Greece, in the Cyclades, is one of my favorite places to sail.

It’s great to spend a week relaxing and swimming in the clear sea with a good book, cold Mythos beer (or a bottle of rosé) and maybe a cigarette.

Tell us the story of a rabbit hole you fell deep into.

Not many people know this; however, I can’t stand the term “rabbit hole.” That said, the story of Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari F40 is one that I inadvertently took a deep dive into and wrote about on Substack. If you follow me, you should know that I’ve always found him to be a hypocritical narcissist, and I had a feeling Ferrari was sugarcoating the actual story.

As it turns out, the “barn find” was identified by a hedge fund, Azimut AHE, and, per usual, Hamilton is full of shit and didn’t find anything in a barn. Azimut located and purchased the car, posting it on Instagram in January of 2025. Hamilton then (allegedly) bought the car from Azimut.

On top of this, Hamilton claimed the engine number is his race number, 44. I went deep enough to confirm that the real engine number is 28302.

In that era, Ferrari didn’t number engines per model or to order. It ran one sequence across everything leaving Maranello. For example, approximately 26000 in 1991 and 28000 in 1992. The real engine number on Hamilton’s F40 fits squarely in their 1992 engine sequencing and has nothing to do with number 44. A specialist also said, “the motor number is completely false. At that time, it was not the way it was numbered.”

So, while the whole barn find, 44 story is nice, it’s bullshit, as it’s simply not how Maranello worked. (IP)

item.title: The Deadline Edition
item.description: On submit buttons, elections, and putting things off.
item.dc:creator: Guest Contributor
item.content:encoded:
Kelly Berold (KB) is based in Paris, where she writes and consults for luxury brands. (She’s also a longtime friend of WITI, and a true information omnivore.) She can be reached at kellyberold@gmail.com.

Kelly here. While most people’s eyes have been on America’s midterm election results, yesterday South Africans also voted in local government elections.

The race wasn’t much of an international story, but domestically, it has been utterly eclipsed by one of the more embarrassing political mishaps in recent memory. I can’t stop thinking about it with equal parts schadenfreude and all-too-knowing compassion.

Here’s the story. Every five years, South Africans vote for the municipal councils that run their cities, towns and districts, which in turn elect their mayors. The race is an early temperature check on national politics, and the first since the ruling African National Congress (ANC), the party of Nelson Mandela, lost the comfortable majority it had held for three decades, in 2024.

To be eligible, all parties had until 5pm on 28 August to submit their candidate lists to the Electoral Commission (the IEC) either in person or through an online portal. Two days out, the ANC was still finalising its online submissions, and at 4:55pm, their team was still uploading. When the deadline came and went, 181 public representative candidates across six municipalities, many of them in the party’s Eastern Cape heartland, were left idle in the system. Apparently, no one managed to press the final submit button.

Take a minute to imagine the party in power in your own country on the phone to a website help centre five minutes before a deadline that could bar their candidates from standing in their own strongholds. Then imagine how thoroughly it would be eviscerated by the public when the news broke. Which is obviously what happened. The ANC blamed a glitch. The IEC said the system was working just fine. The country’s Constitutional Court reversed the ruling two weeks before voting day, forcing the commission to print 6.6 million extra ballots.

Why is this interesting?

Beyond the potentially massive political setback had the ruling stood, or the question of whether UX design can carry the force of electoral law, I can’t think of a better public example of how badly we misjudge deadlines in which we ourselves have the most at stake.

The word “deadline” traces back to the Civil War era, specifically a Confederate prison camp in Georgia, where it marked a physical boundary that any prisoner could be shot for crossing. Printers then borrowed it to refer to the edge of the press bed, beyond which type wouldn’t print. By around 1920, newsrooms were using it as the last moment to file copy. Its meaning has continued to move from place to time, with considerably less morbid repercussions.

Nowadays, we’ve maintained the word, but we’ve crossed the line. Our deadline culture is both more elastic and more relentless, with bigger buffers, but also sometimes seemingly none at all, because now everything is typically asked for unequivocally and indiscriminately ASAP. Deadlines are increasingly arbitrary, over-allocated, and misclassified, yet missing one has become more a moral than a mortal error — doing so feels more like a reflection of your character than the precursor to any real consequences..

The ANC won by arguing evidence of intention, but rival parties jeered that a deadline that bends for whoever goes to court isn’t much of a deadline at all.

I think anyone who has been besieged by their own procrastination knows instinctively, though not always intellectually, that delays are less an issue of discipline than of proper emotional regulation. In a 2013 paper, researchers Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl note that putting things off is really an attempt to repair short-term mood: we do it to avoid how a task makes us feel, whether we’re bored, or fear judgement, or just cannot handle the uncertainty of the outcome. And we all believe, in our little overachieving minds, that the perception we’ve delivered something of quality outweighs our desire for timely completion.

The other thing is that if you miss deadlines often enough, one of two things happens. Either you become convinced you’re a person who can’t be relied on, until it’s baked into your sense of self and becomes harder to change. Or you breeze past enough “urgent” ones without real consequence that your brain decides the rules don’t really apply to you. The paradox is that deadlines carry more weight than ever as markers of performance and persona, and also mean less and less.

A political party, of course, is not subject to the same emotional calculus as a teenager with a school paper. The ANC had to contend with infighting, complex logistics and, it maintains, a real technical obstacle. But the saga is a reminder that even the most established organizations can also miss deadlines that do matter.

Personally, I’m sending this to Colin and Louis at WITI on the day of the vote, two months after deciding to write it, having vowed to start on time and promising myself I would send it by Monday. Deadlines may be too blunt an instrument to ensure we get things done (well-kept rituals and personal systems do a much better job of that). But it’s hard to argue we could do away with them altogether and still keep a sense of order, fairness and consistency. At some point, a button needs to be pushed. (KB)

item.title: The Common vs. Civil Law Edition
item.description: On signatures, Mexico, and identity theft.
item.dc:creator: Guest Contributor
item.content:encoded:
Steve Bryant (SB) is a freelance content strategist and fractional marketing executive, and the author of several WITIs (Jeep edition, Old PC Games edition, more). He currently lives in Mexico City.

Steve here. I was trying to open a bank account in Mexico City the other day when the executive ripped up my signature right in front of me. She tossed the paper into her trash can, then slid another copy of the same form across the desk.

“I’m sorry, can you please sign again.”

I narrowed my eyes, signed again, then slid the paper across her desk. This time she audibly sighed.

“Your signature needs to be the same signature as your passport,” she said.

I remembered the exact moment I’d signed that passport. It was around 10am in a Duane Reade on Flatbush Avenue. I was hungover. I had to sign on one of those tiny little electric signature pads. I explained this to her.

“There’s no way I can duplicate that signature,” I said. “It was nine years ago.”

The executive slid another form across the desk.

“Can you please try again.”

Why is this interesting?

Completing paperwork in Mexico, where I live, is harder than nailing Jell-O to a tree. This doesn’t just apply to opening a bank account, but really anything that requires proving your identity: getting married, buying a house, registering a business. The process is so trying that the only way to survive it, for some, is to document their frustration in a newsletter.

Why, you might ask, is this the case? The answer has little to do with the all too predictable lament of dismissive foreigners—Beautiful country, but so disorganized!— and everything to do with the legal tradition of civil law.

If you’re a citizen of the UK (except Scotland), Canada (except Québec), or the United States (except Louisiana), this won’t be a tradition you’re accustomed to. In those countries, you live under common law. Common law runs on judicial precedent, and courts work by stare decisis — “to stand by things decided.” Judges build the rules case by case, and each decision binds the next.

But if you’re a citizen of Continental Europe, any country in Latin America, or Japan, Korea, or Taiwan, say, you’re living under civil law. Civil law doesn’t run on precedent, it runs on codes: comprehensive statutes that try to anticipate every situation in advance. Judges apply the code, rather than construct doctrine out of accumulated decisions. The tradition is Roman, and was carried into medieval Europe through the universities, before being codified by Napoleon and exported to the Americas by Spain, which brought smallpox, Catholicism, and Roman law, in roughly that order of immediate impact.

For the lowly petitioner trying to open a bank account, the big difference between the two systems comes down to this: civil law codes have to do all the work up front. The prior decisions don’t matter, so the system develops an obsession with proof. The fact of your identity must be proven at the point of any regulated transaction, regardless of how many regulated transactions you’ve made before.

Common law citizens are accustomed to exactly the opposite. You show your ID, sign a form, and the transaction closes. The system doesn’t stop you from lying, it punishes you afterwards. One charming consequence is that in the United States, anybody can be you. Are we not an inventive people, up to and including identity theft?

The other thing is this: common law countries tend to have privatized verification, e.g., title insurance, credit bureaus, and escrow companies. In the U.S., we outsourced the job of trust to private firms that prefer to put a price on the risk that you’re going to lie, rather than certify the truth of your identity. Mexico, instead, kept all that inside the state.

All that is to say that nobody’s going to steal my identity here down below the Rio Grande. Which is good! But it does make it hella difficult to open a bank account. (SB)

item.title: The Monday Media Diet with Dan Mitchell
item.description: On Lydia Kallipoliti, Toraja, in Sulawesi, and Are.na
item.dc:creator: Colin Nagy
item.content:encoded:
Dan Mitchell is creative director at WITI favorite Potato Head in Bali. Happy to have him with us this week. -Colin (CJN)

Tell us about yourself.

I’m Daniel Mitchell, creative director at Potato Head, where I’ve been since 2014. I grew up in Newcastle before moving to London, where I worked as a menswear buyer at Oki-Ni. I later co-founded LN-CC in 2010, as well as several other creative projects in London around that time.

In 2014, I moved to Bali and set up Island of the Gods Records, a label built on cultural exchange between contemporary musicians from the West and traditional Balinese musicians and artists. Soon after, I met Ronald Akili and joined Potato Head as global creative director. We began working towards a shared ambition: creating a zero-waste ecosystem driven by culture. Twelve years later, I’m still here!

During lockdown, I also founded the design studio Space Available. I’m very much interested in creating spaces where people connect and projects with a clear purpose and a positive impact. Potato Head gives me a platform to bring art, architecture, music, food and wellbeing into one cohesive cultural expression—and hopefully do a little good along the way!

Describe your media diet.

It’s largely books, particularly on design and architecture. There aren’t many specialist bookshops in Bali, but Potato Head has a fantastic library, and I’m fortunate to travel regularly, so I tend to bring books home from every trip.

Recently, I’ve been enjoying ABOUT:, an architecture publication from Italy. I also follow the usual suspects, such as Dezeen, ArchDaily, Frame and Emerge, alongside a few Japanese titles and platforms such as Are.na.

What are you reading now?

I’m reading The Architecture of Closed Worlds by Lydia Kallipoliti. It explores the idea of self-sufficient environments, from space capsules to countercultural experiments in architecture and autonomous living.

It’s an interesting exploration of how these closed-loop systems handle energy and resources, including how they turn human waste into something useful. It connects closely with questions we’re exploring at Potato Head: how a place can support itself, what happens to the things we discard, and how waste can become part of another cycle.

What’s your reading strategy when you pick up a print copy of your favorite publication?

I tend to read slowly, from beginning to end. If an image or an idea catches my attention, I mark it with a Post-it so I can return to it later.

I also keep a notebook alongside me for thoughts, ideas and things I’ve learnt. Sometimes those notes relate directly to what I’m reading; other times, something on the page sends my thinking somewhere else. That’s often the most useful part.

Who should everyone be reading that they’re not?

I always return to the Whole Earth Catalog. I first picked it up around 15 years ago and fell deep into the world of Stewart Brand, Buckminster Fuller and the wider counterculture movement of the 1960s.

I’d start there, then explore Fuller’s writing on systems thinking and how we might design a future in synergy with nature. What interests me is the connection between design, ecology and everyday living, and how everything relates to the whole. Those ideas still feel incredibly relevant today.

What is the best non-famous app you love on your phone?

Are.na is probably the closest thing, although I’m not a big app person. I use the usual tools, but as more of life moves onto screens, I find myself wanting to make more room for things I can do with my hands and preserve headspace for thinking and deep work.

Digital tools, including AI, have their uses. I’m just conscious of protecting space for my own thoughts. I don’t feel the need to abandon technology, but I want to be deliberate about how much of my attention it gets.

Plane or train?

Train. I love watching the landscape change as small villages give way to towns and fields give way to cities. There’s something particularly interesting about seeing a country as a whole, travelling through places marked by different historical moments.

That said, I do enjoy long-haul flights. Airports are another story: the queues and procedures feel overdue for a rethink. But once I’m on the plane, I turn off the Wi-Fi and enjoy having nowhere else to be. Half a day alone with my own thoughts has become something I very much enjoy. Given the choice, though, I’d take a long train journey through somewhere new.

What is one place everyone should visit?

Toraja, in Sulawesi. I spent time there researching projects for Potato Head, staying with local families and experiencing some of their ceremonies and daily life.

The architecture and craft were extraordinary, but what stayed with me most was encountering a different relationship with life, death and remembrance. The landscape is beautiful, and there’s a rich culture around ritual food and local ingredients. It’s somewhere I’d encourage people to visit with time, curiosity and respect.

Tell us the story of a rabbit hole you fell deep into.

Indonesia has been my longest rabbit hole. I first came to Bali around twenty years ago with my wife, who is Indonesian, and fell in love with the place and people. That visit eventually became a move, and I’ve now lived here for twelve years.

I was drawn to the possibility of a different way of living: closer to the mountains and ocean, more connected to nature, with ideas of growing my own food and learning about regenerative farming. In many ways, I still feel at the beginning of that adventure.

Bali has changed enormously, but across Indonesia there is so much I’m still learning, from the relationships between people and nature to the rituals, craft traditions and philosophies that shape everyday life. Every project opens another door. Twelve years in, I’m still following those threads.

item.title: The Kenyan Running Edition
item.description: On learning in packs, ground contact, and Iten.
item.content:encoded:
Take the rematch. Everyone has a near miss: the audition you froze in, the race you didn't finish, the challenge that didn't quite get there. This is your 'Rocky II' moment. Redemption is calling. Pick your hype song, set your sights, and make it happen.
link → https://bucketlisterchallenge.com/witi-4

Colin here. I am an on-again, off-again runner. Whenever I’m trying to get more Zone 2 time, running is a very efficient way to get there, so that’s typically when I’ll lace up again. The first two weeks of every comeback generally suck and make me feel worthless. Those minutes are spent lumbering with heavy feet, a bobbling head, and the feeling that I am being charged full price by the world for every mile.

Then the muscle memory kicks in. I remember the stuff I was taught by coaches and good runners in the past; Shorten the stride a little, let my feet land closer under me. Use the balls of my feet, relax my shoulders, and the whole working machine gets quieter. Same lungs, same legs, far less energy (and pain).

At the elite end, that small adjustment may well be the ballgame, though the researchers are careful to call it a hypothesis. A study of 15 elite Kenyan men found ground contact times to be roughly 10% shorter than previously published figures for elite runners at similar speeds, alongside an 8.9% lower oxygen cost. Less time on the ground leaves less time for braking forces from planet earth to slow you down.

Why is this interesting?

Adharanand Finn, who lived in Iten, Kenya (the home of running champions) for six months, describes the Kenyan form as something that comes to them naturally from a childhood spent being active and running around barefoot. Even so, Kenyan runners themselves don’t believe that barefoot running makes them faster.

Another potential answer is more intriguing.

Young runners in Iten train in packs, and through months and years of running with others they learn what different paces feel like, and become masters of the effort behind a specific pace. The faster runner sets the tempo and the slower one practices holding on. Think of the power of spending a season tucked behind someone relaxed and efficient. The cadence, the quiet shoulders and the short contact time get absorbed by osmosis (or survival!) along the way. Biomechanics chatter be damned.

The curriculum also includes patience. One Iten coach told Finn that part of the reason for running slowly is so the body, and hence the mind, doesn’t start to dread training. Easy running is how you earn the right to be relaxed when it gets hard.

The elite hand down more than technique. With little funding for up-and-coming athletes, successful runners often give their training partners shoes and gear, help with transport, and even cover their food.

Which brings me back to my own stride. I have always treated form as a bug to be fixed mid-run, by thinking hard about my shoulders as I go. The Kenyan model suggests form works more like an accent, picked up from whoever you run beside. A better stride may come from spending more time next to people who already have one. Too bad I like to run alone. (CJN)

item.title: The Shoe Leather Edition
item.description: On LVMH, Intern Pierre, and loose engagement rings.
item.dc:creator: Guest Contributor
item.content:encoded:
Alfred Tong (AT) is a London-based writer who has covered luxury for GQ, Esquire and The Sunday Times. He writes Notes by Alfred Tong, where he recently expanded on this same subject.

Alfred here. Vibes. Smells. Feel. Atmosphere. Spilled orange juice on the floor of a big, shiny shop. Something’s off.

There are some things you can only find out if you physically go to the shops. The big brains call it qualitative research. And it can be used to back up your intuition against more conventional data.

Why is this interesting?

This is how ‘Intern Pierre’ bet against LVMH and won. In 2023, Pierre, who runs a small family-office in Europe and writes anonymously as Intern Pierre, shorted the world’s biggest luxury group. “Every fund called me ‘nuts’,” he says.

His first clue about LVMH came at a dinner. His wife’s friends agreed that Tiffany’s premium was no longer worth paying. One said a Tiffany engagement ring would tell her that the guy hadn’t tried, and that he’d also overpaid.

This was the jeweller Arnault had paid almost $16 billion to acquire. At this dinner table, a Tiffany ring had become a sign of not trying very hard. Pierre’s hunch hardened after he observed, out in the real world, that other LVMH brands—Moët, Veuve Clicquot—had become the lazy, or at least the default option.

Pierre says he looks for an “ice cube melting”: a business where “the deterioration has already started” but the numbers haven’t caught up. He listens to his wife and her friends, quizzes former executives and buyers, commissions surveys and visits shops. He doesn’t mistake an anecdote for proof; he looks for the same story in different places.

In July 2025, Goldman Sachs added LVMH to its European conviction list, forecasting 69 per cent upside against 5 per cent downside. The shares rose almost 6 per cent that day. For a short seller, it’s the worst thing that can happen.

I asked whether he wavered. “Lol. I shorted more.” Goldman, he said, “clearly didn’t do much fieldwork”. “I talked to the biggest buyer of these particular products in Europe, and I can tell you they’re not buying this.”

On Rodeo Drive last month, the ground floor of Louis Vuitton’s women’s flagship was moderately busy. The two floors above it were empty. A sales associate told him foot traffic and sales were down almost 30 per cent. At Tiffany, down the road, the customer chair was stained and an engagement ring lay loose in its case.

“Unless my eyes are seeing the wrong thing,” Pierre says, “it’s pretty cut and dry. Either this store’s crowded or it’s not.”

At Dior in Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands this month, nobody greeted him at the door. In the men’s section he found rubbish in a seating area and point-of-sale terminals left out on tables. “Letting me roam freely is amazing for me (and my readers),” he wrote, “and it is generally awful for whatever store I’m allowed to walk through.”

His conviction won out. Since its April 2023 peak, LVMH stock has fallen 57 per cent. Earlier this month, Pierre covered most of his short, for a return of more than 50 per cent.

What does it all mean? That common sense, which often isn’t that common, is still the quickest way to find something out. The trick is having the nerve to trust what you’ve seen with your own eyes. (AT)

item.title: The Monday Media Diet with Claire Stapleton
item.description: On Celebrity Book Club, The Quiet American, and Maggie O’Farrell’s Land
item.dc:creator: Claire Stapleton
item.content:encoded:
Claire Stapleton is a writer and former tech exec. She just published a memoir, Don’t be Evil. Her Substack is Tech Support. Happy to have her with us this week. -Colin (CJN)

Tell us about yourself.

I’m Claire. I worked at Google for a long time, in various writing, comms, and marketing roles, before inadvertently becoming a labor organizer when I, along with a bunch of other women, organized the Google Walkout in a moment of collective rage. This abruptly thrust me into the public sphere as a “tech worker organizer” and critic of Google and Big Tech’s ills writ large—which, naturally, proved difficult to reconcile with my day job as an enthusiastic paid corporate shill. The contradiction didn’t hold for long.

I emerged from my 12-year-long Google bubble/career in 2019, 34 years old, pregnant with baby #2, with zero steer on how to answer the question “now what?” In a sense, I’ve been answering that ever since, with the two most obvious outputs being 1/ Tech Support, my Substack, wherein I help other people grapple with existentially tinged “now what?” questions, and 2/ my memoir, Don’t Be Evil, which was such a massive “life’s work” endeavor that I’m now asking the “now what?” question afresh. I live in Brooklyn with my husband and two sons.

Describe your media diet.

Unhinged. If there are allegations that I’m not a serious person, I’m not beating them here today. I almost never proactively visit major news websites, for better or worse (probably definitely worse). Everything comes to me via feed, group chat, meme account, Reddit, or osmosis, and yet I feel like I’m not missing much in the “discourse.” These past couple of months, putting my book out into the world has given me a bit more professional justification for being so hooked into my phone, but I’m feeling like it’s time to dust off the Brick, reinstate the screen-time limits, and stop donating my brain to Big Tech’s brain-rot experiment.

My afternoon treat, though, is YouTube. I’m drawn to non-famous people who vlog, because the delusion that we’re all the stars of our own TV shows is laid bare there (or maybe not such a delusion–plenty of them now have mansions and a massive spigot of brand deals).. I love these tiny glimpses into worlds I’d never otherwise see: moms with 8+ kids (there are a lot of these), a woman who runs a foster care house, an Orthodox Jewish woman showing life in a neighboring part of Brooklyn, a doctor on 24-hour shifts, and quite a few Mormons.

I open X once a day, mostly to see how the MAGA factions are clashing and turning on each other or strenuously, openly arguing that immigrants, women’s autonomy, and empathy are the main things accelerating the collapse of civilization (the recent “Indian Question” debate was huge for me).

I don’t listen to podcasts very often, since I can’t find a natural place for them in my urban lifestyle. But I am spiritually devoted to Poog, Doomscroll, Celebrity Book Club with Steven & Lily, The Dig Radio, and TrueAnon, the only one I think I’ve ever paid for. Liz Franczak makes me feel strangely safe in a world where everything is connected and none of the connections are good.

What’s the last great book you read?

If I’m being honest, and why not, it’s Buford the Little Bighorn, a picture book by the wonderful author-illustrator of yesteryear Bill Peet. I read it to my six-year-old the other day and was laughing and clapping like a seal. Just a delight.

Because I’m not a total philistine/child, I’ll give an adult answer too: I reread Graham Greene’s The Quiet American while writing my book and was stunned by how relevant it felt. It’s about the very human desire to be part of something larger than ourselves, and the danger of attaching that desire to power. Pyle believes so completely in his own good intentions that he can’t see the harm he’s doing in their name. Obviously, I was thinking about Silicon Valley, and my own years of trusting in Google’s grand mission. But also about what happens when our faith in institutions begins to collapse while our longing for purpose and belonging remains intact. We still want to be part of something bigger. The question is who gets to put that impulse to work, and toward what ends.

What are you reading now?

I’m currently alternating between Meghan O’Gieblyn’s Will and Attention and Maggie O’Farrell’s Land. I read five to ten pages a night before falling asleep, and some nights I have to reread the previous night’s bit. A tidal approach to reading. Both books are gorgeous and lend themselves to it.

What’s your reading strategy when you pick up a print copy of your favorite publication?

We recently let our long-running weekend New York Times delivery lapse, not out of some principled media stance, though that would be cool; we just forgot. So now The New Yorker is the last Print Pub standing in our house (besides alumni magazines and Sports Illustrated Kids).

My strategy is to study the table of contents and contributors intensely, as if I’m about to embark on a rigorous quest of intellectual self-improvement. Then skim Tables for Two, Talk of the Town, and Shouts & Murmurs, maybe pick one whole essay to edify myself, read the first page of the fiction, and call it a day.

Most recently I read and very much enjoyed Gideon Lewis-Kraus’s essay on AI. One insight I loved was that AI has inadvertently demonstrated that another world is materially possible: it hasn’t cured cancer, but it has shown us what happens when you concentrate an almost unimaginable amount of capital, engineering talent, institutional commitment, and political will on a problem. Which raises the obvious question: why do we accept that this kind of mobilization is possible for AI infrastructure but impossible for so many things society broadly wants and needs?

(See, my commitment to edifying myself with one New Yorker essay per week is working.)

Who should everyone be reading that they’re not?

Clare Frances. I love her Substack, Famous and Beloved. I am genuinely interested in stuff like “Harry Styles sighting NYC” and “is Gracie Abrams cool or not,” and strange and stupid Internet drama. but I also want those interests lifted into broader conversation about the world: how fame is trafficked, how taste circulates, how we’re all in the business of making ourselves interesting and marketable. Clare squares this circle for me: I get celebrity gossip, sharp cultural criticism, and an intellectual justification for spending so much of my life online in the first place.

Also Leigh Claire La Berge, whose book Fake Work I loved for its articulation of how contemporary work has become an elaborate performance of productivity whose actual social value is increasingly difficult to discern (tracks with my last couple years at Google!). I just read her recent n+1 essay, “Michel and Mom,” about sifting through her mother’s journals as her mother develops dementia. It’s intellectually rich, tender, haunting.

I gravitate toward people with Cla(i)re in their names, clearly. (Clairely? Ugh.)

What is the best non-famous app you love on your phone?

TrainingPeaks. I’m so ADHD that when I was writing my book, my developmental editor—shoutout Nancy Rawlinson, you’re my queen—became concerned enough about the chaos of my output that she had me account for my time in 30-minute increments in a personal training app. It worked, and now whenever TrainingPeaks sends me a marketing email now about training for a marathon or whatever, I reflect on the physical and emotional endurance challenge of writing a book, how far I’ve come, and how profoundly out of shape I currently feel to write another one.

Plane or train?

The A train in NYC is the central artery of my life. If something’s not on the A, I’m loath to go.

The plane, though, carries an exciting sense of possibility. Between Covid and having little kids, I haven’t traveled that much in the past decade. My older son has a growing list of places he wants to see, assembled from his own media diet and the world outside our house: Rome, Japan, Mexico. Now that my kids are a bit older and suddenly more worldly, the plane has started to seem exciting again: a route to opening the world up.

What is one place everyone should visit?

I grew up in Northern California, but my parents live in Santa Barbara now, and I remain constantly stunned by the beauty and bounty of California and, especially, how casually accessible so much of it is. Case in point: Loon Point in Summerland. You walk down beneath these huge, dramatic cliffs to a beautiful stretch of beach. There are horses around (my kids and I have taken to calling it “Horse Poop Beach,” for reasons that are obvious but only add to the charm), and the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner goes by above you. It’s somehow spectacular and completely commonplace in this part of the world. Wonder!

Tell us the story of a rabbit hole you fell deep into.

I fell deep into Subliminal Jihad’s episodes about the Grateful Dead, which connected some bizarre dots for me personally. My dad grew up in Atherton, California, and knew Lindsey Buckingham and some of the Dead, and I’d always wondered about the relationship between the very establishment Stanford/Palo Alto world and the counterculture flourishing right alongside it.

The podcast offers a darker, more conspiratorial answer, tracing the Dead’s proximity to CIA/MK-Ultra LSD research, Ken Kesey, and the Acid Tests. The provocative thesis: what if the psychedelic counterculture wasn’t so much a rebellion against power as a way of redirecting antiwar political energy into LSD, personal liberation, and extremely long jams?

And once you entertain that possibility, you start wondering what else that feels spontaneous, organic, even liberatory might actually be serving interests you can’t see. You don’t have to buy every conspiracy theory to become a little less confident in the official story of how culture happens. This rabbit hole’s deep, man….
